name: Cyprus
summary: Independent from Britain in 1960; divided since the Turkish invasion of 1974, with a Turkish Cypriot administration in the north recognised only by Turkey.

knownFor.label: Green Line
knownFor.note: UN buffer zone dividing the island.

location.value: The third-largest island in the Mediterranean, with Turkey to the north and Syria and Lebanon to the north-east.

terrain.value: The Troodos mountains in the south-west, the Kyrenia range in the north and the Mesaoria plain between them.

climate.value: Mediterranean, with very mild winters on the coast and warm to hot summers; droughts have become more frequent.

resources.value: Copper (which gave the Latin word for copper) and offshore natural gas found in recent years.

disasters.value: Droughts, which have become more frequent.

population.value: About 1.1 million on the whole island, including about 300,000 in the north (2010 estimate).

urbanisation.value: Nicosia, the capital and largest city, is divided by the Green Line; Limassol and Larnaca are the main harbours.

disease.value: A national health system (GESY) began on 1 June 2019, starting with outpatient services.
disease.source: Lockton, "Cyprus introduces a new national health system" (checked 10 Nov 2026)

migration.value: The 1974 invasion displaced over 150,000 Greek Cypriots and 50,000 Turkish Cypriots; settlers from Turkey were settled in the north.

economicBase.value: Tourism (the largest sector, 14% of GDP), financial services and shipping.

tradeRoutes.value: At the crossroads of Europe, Africa and Asia; joined the EU in 2004.

moneyAndTax.value: The euro replaced the Cypriot pound in 2008; in the 2012–2013 crisis a €10 billion bailout required a large cut to uninsured bank deposits.

inequality.value: Moderate inequality; a large gap between the south and the north.

governmentType.value: A presidential republic: the president is both head of state and head of government.

keyRulers.value: President Archbishop Makarios III, briefly ousted by the 1974 coup.

succession.value: The president is elected by universal suffrage for a five-year term.

institutions.value: House of Representatives; the 1963–64 crisis ended Turkish Cypriot representation in the republic.

stability.value: Intercommunal violence (1963–64); coup and Turkish invasion (1974).

eliteConflict.value: Reunification efforts failed: the Annan Plan was rejected in 2004 and talks collapsed in 2017.

armyAndTech.value: National Guard; Britain keeps two sovereign military bases (Akrotiri and Dhekelia).

majorWars.value: Intercommunal violence (1963–64); a Greek-backed coup and the Turkish invasion (1974).

territoryChange.value: The north is under a Turkish Cypriot administration recognised only by Turkey.

alliancesRivals.value: EU member since 2004; announced in 2024 that it intends to join NATO; a dispute with Turkey over sea zones and gas exploration since 2020.

scienceEducation.value: University of Cyprus (1989) and many private universities.

openness.value: Tourism, finance and shipping; a base for offshore businesses thanks to low taxes.

communicationTransport.value: Coastal motorways and airports at Larnaca and Paphos; crossing between north and south has been possible since April 2003.

religion.value: Most Greek Cypriots are Greek Orthodox Christians; most Turkish Cypriots are Sunni Muslims.

languageWriting.value: Greek and Turkish are both official.

artsArchitecture.value: Architecture shaped by French Gothic and Italian Renaissance styles; the Neolithic village of Khirokitia is a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

socialStructure.value: Greek Cypriots 77%, Turkish Cypriots 18% and others 5% (2001); Armenians, Latins and Maronites are recognised minorities.

sharedIdentity.value: Greek Cypriots and Turkish Cypriots share many traditional foods, drinks and ways of life.

dailyLife.value: Halloumi cheese, meze dishes, souvla and souvlaki.

neighbours.value: Turkey, Syria, Lebanon, Israel, Egypt, Greece.

ideasReligions.value: Greek Orthodox Christianity and Sunni Islam.

riseSignals.value: Independence (1960) after an armed campaign by EOKA, founded in 1955.

declineSignals.value: Division of the island (1974) and the 2012–2013 financial crisis.

outcome.value: Still divided: the Republic of Cyprus and the self-declared Turkish Republic of Northern Cyprus (recognised only by Turkey).

overallCertainty.value: The status of the north is disputed.
